summary: A proposed first part of a Network Standard Graphics Protocol from the Network Graphics Group. It describes the stream of 8-bit bytes sent from an application on a serving host to a display package on a using host, covering only the simplest forms of graphics data. It was replaced by RFC 493.

eli5.summary: The first draft of the rules for sending pictures across the network as a line of numbers, starting with just the simplest shapes.

subtitle: Simple graphics commands for the early network

tldr.problem: The ARPANET had no standard way for one computer to send graphics data to another computer's display. Each system used its own format.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Graphics Group proposed a simple protocol using 8-bit bytes, where a command byte followed by arguments tells the receiving computer what to draw. Level 0 uses only basic commands: move, draw, dot, and text.
tldr.outcome: Level 0 provided a minimum viable graphics protocol that even simple systems could implement quickly for experimentation.

today: RFC 292 is historic and was superseded by RFC 493. This Level 0 protocol never saw widespread use, but it pioneered thinking about how to transmit graphics across the early network.

sections.title: Graphics on the Network
sections.content:
RFC 292 describes the first level of a proposed Network Standard Graphics Protocol, a way for a computer to send graphics data across the ARPANET to a display device. The document reflects decisions made by the Network Graphics Group at a meeting in late November 1971.

This protocol covers only the data sent from a serving host (where the application runs) to a using host (which displays the graphics). It does not include the reverse direction (user input) or how to establish the connection.
sections.eli5: This is the rule book for sending a picture to another computer by listing all the things to draw.

sections.title: Level 0: The Simplest Commands
sections.content:
The protocol uses a stream of 8-bit bytes. Each command consists of a command byte followed by zero or more arguments. Level 0 is intentionally simple so that even the least powerful hosts can implement it quickly.

Level 0 commands include: Erase (clear screen), Move Absolute or Move Relative (position without drawing), Draw Absolute or Draw Relative (draw a line), Dot Absolute or Dot Relative (draw a point), Text (display text), and End of Picture.
sections.eli5: You can tell the computer "move your pen here," "draw a line," "put a dot," and "write this word." No storing special states—just the current command and where the pen is.

sections.title: Coordinates and Data Format
sections.content:
Graphics use a logical coordinate system where the screen ranges from -1/2 to slightly less than +1/2 in both X and Y, with the origin at the center. Each computer translates these logical coordinates to its own physical display.

Coordinates are sent as two-byte values using two's complement notation. Text is sent as a count followed by that many 8-bit bytes, using Network ASCII. The protocol reserves opcodes 128 to 255 for future protocol commands.
sections.eli5: The numbers are always between -0.5 and 0.5, and every computer figures out how to fit them on its own screen. Words are sent as a number saying "four letters follow" and then those four letters.

sections.title: Levels and Future Work
sections.content:
The protocol is organized into levels. Any host implementing level N must support all lower levels. This allows sites to implement levels incrementally. Level 0 requires no internal storage for modes or stacks, so a very simple implementation—even in hardware—should be possible.

Higher levels are planned to add more capabilities, but implementers are assured that understanding level N does not require knowledge of level N+1.
sections.eli5: If a computer learns level 0, it can talk to any other computer. More powerful computers can learn level 1 and 2 later for fancy stuff, but they still remember level 0.

references.text: Michener, J., et al., "Graphics Protocol - Level 0 Only," RFC 292, January 1972.
